primary_claim: A zero-sum joint scoring rule that pits predictive agents against each other empirically prevents performative prediction (self-fulfilling manipulation of outcomes) in a toy environment: both implementations tested yield rising principal utility and non-performative predictive accuracy throughout training, whereas unconstrained training shows non-performative accuracy collapsing after an initial rise and principal utility plateauing.

models.family: toy neural net (randomly initialized MLP predictor)

effect.metric: principal's utility and non-performative predictive accuracy over training, zero-sum objective vs. no-intervention baseline
effect.value: zero-sum objectives (exact and dropout variants) show continuously rising principal utility and non-performative accuracy; no-intervention baseline shows the largest initial gain in performative accuracy but non-performative accuracy then drops off sharply and principal utility plateaus

contradicts_or_qualifies: Improves on prior mechanisms for honest prediction: 'Decision Markets with Good Incentives' (Chen et al.) requires randomizing with full support, including commitment to taking arbitrarily bad actions, while 'Decision Scoring Rules' requires directly optimizing a principal's utility function, which the author argues runs into known reward-hacking-style problems
stated_future_work: Resolve the open issue of incentives when agents have different (private-information) beliefs
Expand the empirical segment using larger models in a more complex environment

Run an experiment using population-based training to induce performative prediction evaluated with human feedback, to demonstrate the model learns to maximize predictability rather than human preferences
Explore applying zero-sum competition ('within-episode myopia') to other alignment problems beyond prediction
limitations_stated: One notable theoretical result, for the case where agents have private information, eluded the author and remains unsolved
Theorem 4 (disagreement-seeking decision rule) relies heavily on all agents knowing the ground truth; even small amounts of prediction noise can cause the principal to choose arbitrarily bad actions
The author is 'slightly bearish' on expanding empirical work with larger models, doubting it would reveal much about applications to goal-directed AI agents
quote: We can see that both implementations of a zero-sum objective perform very similarly, increasing in predictive accuracy both for the performatively chosen action and across all actions.
